Checking local flat-foldability at every interior vertex: Kawasaki holds everywhere, but Maekawa fails at two vertices.
- Vertex 21 (0.125,0.125): creases at -135,0,45,90 deg are all V (0 M / 4 V; |M-V| must be 2).
- Vertex 22 (0.15625,0.15625): 2 M / 2 V (|M-V| = 0).
Both share the diagonal crease 21-22 (assigned V); its assignment appears flipped, so as given the pattern cannot be folded flat.

All creases radiate from the boundary vertex 0 = (0.5, 1); every other vertex lies on the paper boundary. So there are no interior vertices, and no Kawasaki or Maekawa test applies anywhere. Whether the pattern folds comes down to whether the fan of sectors around vertex 0 can be stacked, which works like folding a line segment (1D).

Going clockwise from the edge to vertex 8, the sector angles are:
50.91, 12.53, 12.53, 14.04, 14.04, 12.53, 12.53, 50.91 degrees.
The creases between them are (to v6) M, (v3) M, (v5) V, (v1) M, (v4) M, (v2) M, (v7) M.

1D flat-foldability test (crimps and end folds):
- End folds: impossible, because each end sector (50.91) is larger than its neighbour.
- Crimps: the only possible crimp is the 12.53 sector between the creases to v3 (M) and v5 (V). Doing it leaves the sectors 50.91, 14.04, 14.04, 12.53, 12.53, 50.91 with the creases M, M, M, M, M.
- After that, every remaining crease is a mountain. No crimp is possible, because each smallest sector sits between two creases of the same direction, and end folds are still impossible.
- The test ends before everything is folded, so the fan cannot be folded flat without paper passing through paper.

So the pattern is not flat-foldable. Every interior-vertex local condition holds trivially because there are no interior vertices. The failure is in the layer ordering of the whole fan, which is a global failure.

```json
{"foldable": false, "violation_vertices": []}
```

The CP folds flat. The diagonal x=y is mountain along its whole length, and three perpendicular lines (x+y=0.5, 1, 1.5) cross it. Every vertex has four 90-degree sectors, so Kawasaki holds, and each has 3 mountains and 1 valley, so Maekawa holds. Folding the diagonal (the upper-left half goes behind) gives a 2-layer triangle strip. The three perpendicular creases split this strip into four equal segments of length sqrt(2)/4, which stack on top of each other. With face 6 kept face-up, the stack from bottom to top is 7,6,4,5,0,1,3,2: the last segment is tucked between the second and third segments.

This is the waterbomb base. Kawasaki holds at the center (45-90+45-45+90-45=0), and Maekawa holds too (4 V, 2 M). The corners 0 and 4 meet at (0,0), the corners 2 and 3 meet at (1,0), and the midpoints 5 and 6 both land at (0.5,0).

Design: the classic bird base, which is a 22.5-degree design. The four flaps come from the four corners. Each corner flap is a circle of radius 0.5, and the four circles touch at the edge midpoints. When folded, the edge midpoints all land on one hub point on the axis. The two petal corners point one way and the two leg corners point the other, and every corner tip is 0.5 from the hub. Every pair of tips is therefore 1.0 apart, which gives scale m = 0.5 (the best known circle packing for four equal flaps). Every crease is at 0, 45, 90, 22.5 or 67.5 degrees. I checked the flat fold by computer: Kawasaki holds (the folded face transforms are consistent), Maekawa holds at every interior vertex, and a layer order was found that satisfies taco-tortilla, taco-taco and transitivity. The M/V assignment comes from that layer order.

Reasoning: Three equal flaps on a square. In box pleating, flap regions are L-infinity squares, and three points in the unit square can be at most L-infinity distance 1 apart. That gives a best possible scale of m = 1/16 = 0.0625, against a circle-packing optimum of about 0.0647.

I place flaps of length 0.5 at the paper corners, with the hub along the midlines. Each corner's axis coordinate is max(|dx|,|dy|) from the corner, so every flap is 0.5 long. This is the square folded flat into 1/8: fold in half along x=0.5, then along y=0.5, then along the diagonal. It is made only of simple folds, so a valid layer order exists. The three target leaves are matched to three of the four corner flaps, and the fourth flap is spare. Any two tips are 1.0 apart in the tree, which is at least 16m, so m = 1/16.

The pattern uses a 2x2 grid, with all creases at 0, 90 and 45 degrees and all vertices on lattice points. At the centre vertex there are 5 valley and 3 mountain creases, so Maekawa holds (5 - 3 = 2).

The target is a kite with a 90 deg corner, short sides 0.414214 (sqrt2-1) and long sides 0.765367. That is a kite base scaled by 1/sqrt2. To get it, fold all four corners to the centre (a blintz, which leaves a square of side 1/sqrt2). Then kite-fold the blintzed square from its corner at (0,0.5): two 22.5-degree bisector folds pass through the base layer and through the blintz flaps underneath them. On the flipped flaps those folds are reflected and become mountains.

Fold the paper in half twice (book fold, then book fold again). First a valley fold along x=0.5 brings the right half onto the left half. Then a valley fold along y=0.5 brings the top half down. The result is a 0.5 x 0.5 square, which is 1/4 of the paper's area, and all four paper corners land on the same corner of that square.
Crease assignments on the unfolded sheet: both segments of x=0.5 are V. The left segment of y=0.5 is V. The right segment of y=0.5 is M, because that layer was face-down during the second fold. The centre vertex therefore has 3 V and 1 M (Maekawa holds), and all its angles are 90 degrees (Kawasaki holds).

Inscribe the largest equilateral triangle in the square: vertices (0,0), (1,t), (t,1) with t = 2 - sqrt(3) = 0.267949. Its side is 1.035276 and its area is about 0.4641, which is at least 0.3.

The three corner flaps fold onto the triangle with valley folds along its sides. The flap at (1,1) fits completely inside. The flaps at (1,0) and (0,1) fold across the 15-degree and 75-degree sides, and a small tip of each sticks out past the third side. That tip folds back along the third side's line. On the paper this gives a mountain crease from (1,t) to (4*sqrt(3) - 6, 0) = (0.928203, 0), and a matching one from (t,1) to (0, 0.928203). These are mountain folds because the flap has already been flipped.

Every crease endpoint is on the paper boundary, so there are no interior vertices. A valid layer order (bottom to top) is: main triangle, (1,1) flap, then the side flaps with their tips on top. The side flaps sit in disjoint wedges, so they do not overlap each other.

Leaf pairs: leg-leg 6, head-leg 4, abdomen-leg 5, head-abdomen 3. Eight points in the unit square with pairwise L-inf distance > 1/2 are impossible: split the square into four 1/2 x 1/2 quadrants, and each quadrant can hold only one such point. So 6m <= 1/2, which gives m <= 1/12.
To reach m = 1/12, put the legs on the 3x3 half-grid without its centre. Put the abdomen at (0.5, 5/12) and the head at (0.5, 2/3). Abdomen to nearest leg = 5/12 = 5m. Head to nearest leg = 1/3 = 4m. Head to abdomen = 1/4 = 3m. Checked numerically: min ratio = 1/12.

In every case the top and bottom faces had a fixed parity (tip8 has two valid orders, but both give the same colours). The top face shows front if it is front-up. Every crease is a multiple of 22.5 degrees, and there are odd multiples (22.5 and 67.5 degrees), so this is a 22.5-degree design (a bird-base variant with a 1/12 border) and not box pleating. Some vertices, such as 0.37796116 and 0.04881554, are irrational, so no 1/N lattice with N <= 512 fits them (grid = null). There are no Pythagorean-triple directions.

Crease directions: 0/90/45/135 degrees (box-pleated), plus slopes 3/4 and -4/3 (36.87 and 126.87 degrees), 1/2 and 2 (26.57/63.43 degrees, here 63.43), and 1/3 (18.43 degrees). Folding the CP face by face (reflecting across creases) puts all four corners at one point (axis coordinate 0), the paper center at 0.2929, and all edge midpoints / diagonal hinge points at 0.5 (the closed top of the base). Level-set analysis: the four corner flaps stay separate up to s=0.5, where everything merges into one hub; the paper center is a separate local extremum (a short flap) starting at 0.2929 and also joining the hub at 0.5. So this is the bird base: four long flaps of length 0.5 and one short central flap of length 0.5-0.2929=0.2071.

Folding the CP by composing reflections across creases puts every point on one axis (the folded y coordinate). The four paper corners all land at axis coordinate 1.0. The centre, the even-numbered midline vertices and the boundary midpoints all land at 0.5. The odd-numbered midline vertices (0.0625 off-grid along the four midlines, 16 of them) land at 0.4375.
The level set at 0.5 is connected: its contours run around each 0.4375 minimum and through the centre. That makes it a single hub. Above 0.5, the level sets split into four separate arcs, one around each corner, so there are four corner flaps of length 0.5. Each 0.4375 vertex is an isolated local minimum, so each one is a short pleat flap of length 0.0625 hanging off the hub.

I folded the crease pattern in code by reflecting each face across the creases it shares with its neighbours. In the folded state all of the paper's boundary lies on one line (largest deviation from it is 2e-6), and that line is the axis. I projected every point of the paper onto the axis and built the Reeb graph of that height function: the connected pieces of paper at each level are merged into one node. Nodes with only two neighbours were then removed, keeping the total length along each path. The result has 6 leaves (a head, four legs and a tail, matching a lizard) joined by 4 branch points.
